content: 1. The ketogenic diet (KD) was generally well-tolerated by patients. However, three cases discontinued the diet due to poor tolerability, despite the absence of tumor progression. 2. Three patients exhibited stable disease at six weeks, with disease stability extending to 11, 12, and 13 weeks, respectively. 3. A trend was observed suggesting longer progression-free survival (PFS) in patients who maintained stable ketosis. 4. Among patients who received bevacizumab salvage therapy at the first progression while continuing the KD, a higher response rate was noted. 5. The authors concluded that the KD alone did not demonstrate significant clinical activity in recurrent glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). However, they suggested that combining the KD with other treatment modalities, such as radiotherapy or anti-angiogenic treatments, warrants further investigation (Rieger 2014). 6. A clinical center with extensive experience in ketogenic therapy for adults with refractory epilepsy proposed the modified Atkins diet (MAD) as a safer, more tolerable, and feasible alternative to the calorie-restricted KD for adult oncology patients. 7. The MAD was used in eight adult glioma cases (three GBM, one anaplastic astrocytoma, and four low-grade gliomas) associated with seizure disorders. The diet was well-tolerated without significant toxicity. 8. Seven participants achieved improved seizure control and continued the diet for two to 24 months, while one participant discontinued the diet after three months due to a lack of antiseizure efficacy. 9. At the time of publication, all participants were alive, and the survival rates for those with GBM were comparable to the expected median survival for their respective disease stages (Strowd 2015). 10. The KD is a high-fat, low-carbohydrate, adequate-protein diet first reported as an effective treatment for children with intractable epilepsy in the 1920s (Wilder 1921). 11. The diet was developed based on the observation that extended fasting improved seizure control, and this effect could be replicated by altering macronutrient intake to induce a metabolic shift from carbohydrate to fat as the primary energy source (Neal 2010). 12. Various forms of the KD are currently used in clinical therapy for adults and children with drug-resistant epilepsy, forming the basis of KD regimens in glioma management. 13. All KD regimens require a dietetic prescription tailored to meet the individual’s nutritional needs, with the choice of regimen determined by feeding habits, patient preference, and practical application in the individual’s social setting. 14. Medical and biochemical screening is required before initiating therapy, with regular monitoring throughout the treatment (Kossoff 2009). 15. Evidence supporting the efficacy of the KD in improving seizure control comes from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in children with intractable epilepsy (Neal 2008), adult case series (Barborka 1930), and single-arm adult trials (Ye 2015). 16. The classical KD is based on the original principles described in the 1920s (Wilder 1921). Meals and snacks are planned to provide a consistent ratio of ketogenic fat to anti-ketogenic carbohydrate and protein. 17. Carbohydrate intake is limited, and protein is kept to the minimum requirement for growth in children or adequacy in adults. 18. In children, fat-to-carbohydrate/protein ratios of 3:1 (87% of total dietary energy from fat) and 4:1 (90% of total energy from fat) may be required for optimal seizure control (Cervenka 2013). 19. In older children and adults, a 3:1 or 2:1 ratio (80% of total energy from fat) may provide adequate protein to meet minimal requirements (Neal 2012). 20. Most fat in the KD is provided as long-chain triglycerides (e.g., olive oil, other vegetable oils, butter, cream, and nuts). 21. Classical KD regimens require all foods to be weighed and calculated to ensure consistency in the prescribed macronutrient ratio for each meal and snack. 22. The medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) KD, introduced in the 1970s, provides 60% of dietary energy as MCT (Huttenlocher 1971). 23. MCT KD regimens are calculated to deliver a consistent proportion of energy from MCT (30% to 60%), long-chain triglycerides, protein, and carbohydrate. 24. MCTs are more efficiently converted into ketones than long-chain triglycerides, allowing for a lower total fat percentage and increased carbohydrate and protein allowances. 25. The modified Atkins diet (MAD), introduced in 2003, is based on the popular low-carbohydrate Atkins diet for weight loss. 26. The MAD provides a more liberal ketogenic approach, focusing on strict control of carbohydrate intake (10 g to 20 g per day) with normal portions of protein foods and liberal addition of fats to appetite (Kossoff 2013). 27. The low glycaemic index treatment (LGIT), devised in 2002, is based on the knowledge that acute carbohydrate intake rapidly ends the protective effect of the KD (Pfeifer 2005). 28. Carbohydrate intake in the LGIT provides around 10% of total energy, with sources restricted to foods that produce relatively small changes in blood glucose levels (glycaemic index less than 50). 29. Regular monitoring of seizures, associated symptoms, weight, and ketosis (via blood or urine) enables appropriate adjustments to the KD to optimize seizure outcomes. 30. A three-month trial of an appropriately formulated KD is generally sufficient to determine its effectiveness and long-term viability for an individual (Fitzsimmons 2015). 31. The development of more liberal KDs, such as MAD and LGIT, has made ketogenic therapy more practical and sustainable for both adults and children. 32. Publications assessing the impact of KD on outcomes in central nervous system (CNS) cancer patients are limited to anecdotal case reports and retrospective series. 33. While some encouraging results have been reported, conclusions are limited by the small number of patients, potential selection bias, and lack of prospective validation. 34. Nebeling (1995) reported the first metabolic therapy for human malignant brain tumors. 35. Two pediatric patients with non-resectable, advanced-stage astrocytoma who consumed a 60% MCT KD demonstrated reduced tumor activity on PET scans and clinical improvement in one case. 36. Zuccoli (2010) published a case report of an elderly GBM patient who received an adjuvant calorie-restricted classical KD with standard GBM therapy post-partial resection. 37. After two months of treatment, no discernible tumor tissue was detected on imaging, and the patient remained in good general health with no neurological complications. 38. However, 10 weeks after discontinuing the strict dietary approach, the tumor recurred. 39. An energy-restricted KD was used as monotherapy in two adult GBM cases with documented tumor progression, 14 and 20 months after their initial diagnosis. 40. One case progressed after four weeks, while the other had stable disease at six weeks but experienced progression after 12 weeks of diet therapy (Schwartz 2015). 41. The study authors suggested several explanations for the limited benefit, including failure to maintain serum glucose in the target range of 50 mg to 70 mg/dL or the possibility that KD alone may not effectively reduce tumor growth rates. 42. A retrospective review of 53 GBM cases undergoing treatment with surgery, radiation therapy, and temozolomide reported that six patients following a KD had lower mean blood glucose levels compared to those consuming a standard diet. 43. This benefit was evident even in patients on KD in conjunction with high-dose steroids (Champ 2014). 44. A study examining the feasibility of KD in 20 cases of recurrent GBM concluded that it was safe and relatively well-tolerated. 45. Three cases discontinued the diet due to poor tolerability.
